mainTopic: Oaths and loss when a lender loses the משכון: who swears first, and does losing the משכון cancel the loan?
overview: The משנה discusses a lender who lost the משכון he was holding, where the two sides argue about its value. The גמרא first asks which case the משנה's line 'the one holding the deposit swears' refers to. שמואל, רבי חייא בר רב and רבי יוחנן say it refers to the last case of the first section. There the oath really belongs to the borrower, but the רבנן moved it to the lender. With רב אשי's ruling that both sides swear, the line only tells us that the lender swears first. Next, שמואל rules that if a lender took one cheap item, like a sickle handle, for a big loan and lost it, the whole loan is lost. רב נחמן and the חכמי נהרדעא extend this rule to two items. The גמרא challenges שמואל from our משנה and answers that the משנה is a case where the lender said explicitly that the item covers only its own value. Finally, the גמרא asks whether שמואל's rule is an argument between רבי אליעזר and רבי עקיבא, and starts to work out the exact case of their argument. That discussion continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Which case does the משנה's last line refer to?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which case the משנה's closing line ('who swears? the one holding the deposit') is talking about. It shows that it can't be the סיפא, because there the lender would swear anyway.
steps.simpleTranslation: גמרא: Which case is this about? If you say the last case, you don't need the משנה to tell us that. We would know it anyway, because in that case the oath is on the lender already!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wants to know which case the משנה's line 'the one holding the deposit swears' belongs to. It tests one option, the סיפא, and shows that option makes the line pointless.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the סיפא, the borrower is the one claiming the collateral was worth more, so the lender is the defendant. By normal rules, the lender would already be the one to swear. So if the line meant the סיפא, the משנה would be telling us something obvious. The line must be teaching something new somewhere else.

keyTerms.meaning: On which one? (Which case is this about?)
The last part of a משנה
Let him get it from... (we already know it from another reason)

phrases.english: GEMARA: To which case is this referring?
phrases.notes: He means the משנה's closing line: 'Who swears? The one who had the deposit.'

phrases.english: If you say it refers to the latter clause –
then derive it from the fact that the oath is on the lender anyway!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens the גמרא on the משנה.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which case in the משנה does 'מי נשבע? מי שהפקדון אצלו' apply to?
steps.kashyaTarget: The option that the line refers to the סיפא
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: In the סיפא the lender already swears by normal rules, so the line would add nothing.

steps.title: Three אמוראים: it refers to the first section
steps.stepSummary: שמואל, רבי חייא בר רב and רבי יוחנן all answer that the line refers to the רישא.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: it goes on the first section. רבי חייא בר רב said the same: the first section. רבי יוחנן also said: the first section.
steps.whatsHappening: Three different אמוראים give the same answer: the line about who swears belongs to the רישא, not the סיפא.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying it goes on the רישא avoids the problem from step 1. In the רישא the oath would normally fall on the borrower, so telling us the lender swears is something new. The fact that three great אמוראים say the same thing shows how firm this answer is.

keyTerms.meaning: The first part of a משנה
And so too said... (another rabbi agrees)

phrases.english: Shmuel said: It refers to the first clause.

phrases.aramaic: וְכֵן אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר רַב: אַרֵישָׁא.
phrases.english: And similarly Rabbi Chiyya bar Rav said: To the first clause.
And similarly Rabbi Yochanan said: To the first clause.

steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The line refers to the רישא.

steps.title: What do they mean by 'the first section'?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks which exact case in the רישא the אמוראים meant.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for more detail. The רישא has several cases, so which one did the אמוראים mean? This question sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The very first case in the משנה ends with 'פטור' (no oath at all). So the line about who swears can't refer to that case. The גמרא needs to point to a case in the רישא where someone actually has to swear.

phrases.english: What is meant by 'the first clause'?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for clarification of the answer in step 2.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which specific case in the רישא is meant.

steps.title: The last case of the first section: the oath moved to the lender
steps.stepSummary: It is the סיפא דרישא. The lender says 'I lent a סלע and it was worth a שקל.' The borrower says 'It was worth three דינרין.' By Torah logic the borrower should swear, but the רבנן moved the oath onto the lender.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is the last case of the first section. The lender says: 'I lent you a סלע on it, and it was worth a שקל.' The other one (the borrower) says: 'No, you lent me a סלע on it, and it was worth three דינרין.' In that case there is an oath. The oath really belongs on the borrower, but the רבנן took it off the borrower and put it on the lender.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא names the exact case: the last case of the first section, where the borrower says the collateral was worth three דינרין. Here the oath belongs on the borrower by normal rules, but the רבנן moved it to the lender.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סלע is four דינרין and a שקל is two. The borrower admits he still owes one דינר but denies the second one. That is a classic מודה במקצת, so by normal rules the borrower would swear. That is exactly why the משנה needs to tell us 'the one holding the deposit swears': it is a new rule that the רבנן made.

keyTerms.meaning: The last part of the first section
The רבנן took it (the oath) away

steps.whatToRemember: The line 'מי שהפקדון אצלו נשבע' teaches a rabbinic shift. The borrower should have sworn, but the רבנן moved the oath to the lender, who held the collateral.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up 'רישא' with the very first case of the משנה. The גמרא means the LAST case inside the first section (סיפא דרישא).

phrases.english: The latter part of the first clause:
'I lent you a sela on it'
phrases.notes: 'On it' means on the collateral the borrower gave.

phrases.english: 'and it was worth a shekel,'
and the other one says: 'Not so,'
'rather, you lent me a sela on it'
'and it was worth three dinars' – he is liable to swear.
phrases.notes: The borrower admits owing one דינר and denies one, so this is admitting part of the claim.

phrases.english: For the oath really belongs with the borrower,
but the Rabbis took it from the borrower
and placed it on the lender.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the clarifying question of step 3.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The case is the סיפא דרישא, where the borrower claims the collateral was worth three דינרין. There the רבנן moved the oath from the borrower to the lender.
steps.whyThisMatters: It explains why the משנה needed to say who swears. It is teaching a rabbinic change from the normal oath rules.

steps.title: With רב אשי's view, the line tells us who swears first
steps.stepSummary: Based on רב אשי's ruling that both sides swear, the משנה is read as telling us who swears first. The lender swears first that the collateral is not in his possession, so the borrower doesn't swear and then the lender produces it.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now that רב אשי said what we hold: this one (the lender) swears that the collateral is not in his possession, and that one (the borrower) swears how much it was worth. So this is what the משנה means: Who swears first? The one who had the deposit. Otherwise, this one (the borrower) might swear, and then the other one (the lender) brings out the deposit.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new way to read the משנה. It is based on רב אשי's ruling that both the lender and the borrower swear. The line now only tells us the order: the lender swears first.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, the line meant that ONLY the lender swears instead of the borrower. Now both swear, each about something different. The lender swears that he no longer has the collateral, and the borrower swears about its value. The lender goes first because the borrower might swear about the value, and then the lender could bring out the collateral, so everyone sees what it was really worth and the borrower's oath may turn out false.

keyTerms.meaning: We hold (this is the accepted rule)

steps.whatToRemember: There are two readings of 'מי שהפקדון אצלו'. (1) The oath moves from the borrower to the lender. (2) With רב אשי's ruling, both swear, and the line only tells us the lender swears first.

phrases.english: And now that Rav Ashi said
that we hold
this one swears that it is not in his possession
and that one swears how much it was worth –
phrases.notes: The first 'this one' is the lender; 'that one' is the borrower.

phrases.english: this is what the משנה is saying:
Who swears first?
The one with whom the deposit was.
Lest this one swear,
and then the other one bring out the deposit.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second reading of the משנה's line, replacing the 'oath was moved' reading of step 4.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Following רב אשי's ruling that both parties swear, the משנה's line means that the lender, who held the deposit, swears first that it is not in his possession.

steps.title: שמואל: losing a small pledge can cancel a huge loan
steps.stepSummary: שמואל rules that if someone lent 1,000 זוזים and took a sickle handle as a משכון, losing the handle means losing the whole 1,000. If he took two handles, this rule does not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said: If someone lent his friend a thousand זוזים and took a sickle handle from him as a pledge, and the handle got lost, he lost the thousand זוזים. But if he took two handles, he does not lose everything.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts a new topic: a ruling from שמואל about a lost משכון. Taking a single small item for a big loan is treated as if that item stands for the entire loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A sickle handle is worth almost nothing compared to 1,000 זוזים. The fact that the lender accepted it anyway shows the item was taken to stand for the whole debt, so losing it wipes out the whole debt. With two handles, neither one alone stands for the whole loan, so losing one does not cancel everything.

keyTerms.meaning: Took as a pledge (משכון) to secure a loan
The handle of a sickle, a cheap item
A thousand זוזים, a large sum

steps.whyThisMatters: This sets up the whole discussion. Sometimes a משכון is not just security for its own value but stands in for the entire loan.

phrases.english: Shmuel said:

phrases.aramaic: הַאי מַאן דְּאוֹזְפֵיהּ אַלְפָּא זוּזֵי לְחַבְרֵיהּ,
phrases.english: One who lent a thousand zuz to his friend,
and took from him a sickle handle as a pledge;
if the sickle handle was lost,
he lost the thousand zuz.
But with two handles, no.
phrases.notes: If he took two handles and lost one, he does not lose the whole loan.

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר שְׁמוּאֵל: הַאי מַאן דְּאוֹזְפֵיהּ אַלְפָּא זוּזֵי לְחַבְרֵיהּ
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Opens a new topic connected to lost pledges, after the discussion of oaths about a lost משכון.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A single cheap משכון taken for a large loan stands for the whole loan; losing it cancels the entire debt. With two items this does not apply.

steps.title: רב נחמן: even with two handles, each one covers half
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן says that even with two handles, each handle stands for half the loan. Losing one loses 500, and losing both loses everything. But if the two items were a handle and a piece of silver, this does not apply.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: Even with two handles, if one was lost he lost five hundred, and if the other was lost too he lost all of it. But with a handle and a piece of silver, no.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן goes further than שמואל. He applies the same idea to two handles by splitting the loan between them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב נחמן, two equal cheap items each stand for half the loan, so each loss cancels half. But when one item is a valuable piece of silver, the lender was really relying on the silver. So losing the cheap handle does not cancel half the loan.

keyTerms.meaning: Five hundred, half of the thousand
A piece of silver, a valuable item

phrases.english: And Rav Nachman said:
Even with two handles:
if one was lost, he lost five hundred,
if the other was lost, he lost all of it.
But a handle and a piece of silver, no.
phrases.notes: Here losing the handle does not cost him half, because he was counting on the silver.

steps.triggerLanguage: וְרַב נַחְמָן אָמַר: אֲפִילּוּ תַּרְתֵּי קַתָּאתֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with שמואל's limit and extends his rule to two handles.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: With two equal cheap pledges, each covers half the loan. A cheap item paired with a valuable item does not work this way.

steps.title: The חכמי נהרדעא: even a handle and a piece of silver
steps.stepSummary: The נהרדעי extend the rule further. Even with a handle and a piece of silver, losing the silver loses half the loan, and then losing the handle loses everything.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Sages of נהרדעא say: Even with a handle and a piece of silver, if the silver was lost he lost half, and if the handle was lost he lost all of it.
steps.whatsHappening: A third opinion pushes the rule even further than רב נחמן did, to the case of a handle together with silver.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For the נהרדעי, it does not matter that the two items have very different values. Each still stands for half the loan. So losing the silver cancels half, and losing the handle afterward cancels the rest.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages of the city of נהרדעא

steps.whatToRemember: There are three levels. שמואל: one cheap item stands for the whole loan. רב נחמן: two cheap items each stand for half. נהרדעי: even a cheap item plus silver each stand for half.

phrases.english: The Nehardeans say:
Even a handle and a piece of silver:
if the silver was lost, he lost half,
if the handle was lost, he lost all of it.
phrases.notes: Meaning once both are gone, the whole loan is gone.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Disagrees with רב נחמן's limit and extends the rule to a handle with silver.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Even a cheap item paired with a valuable one: each covers half the loan.

steps.title: Challenge to שמואל from our משנה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes our משנה. A lost משכון worth less than the loan does not cancel the debt; the borrower is still liable for the difference. According to שמואל, the borrower should say 'you already got paid with the משכון.'
steps.simpleTranslation: We learned: 'I lent you a סלע on it and it was worth a שקל,' and the other says, 'No, you lent me a סלע on it and it was worth three דינרים.' He is liable. But according to שמואל, let him say to him: 'You already received it!'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges שמואל using the case from our משנה, where a lost משכון did not wipe out the loan.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In the משנה, both sides agree the loan was a סלע and the משכון was worth less. Yet the borrower is still liable for the gap. According to שמואל, losing a cheap משכון should cancel the whole loan, so the borrower should owe nothing at all.

keyTerms.meaning: A coin worth half a סלע, two דינרים

phrases.english: We learned: "I lent you a sela on it
and it was worth a shekel,"
and the other one says: "Not so,
rather, you lent me a sela on it
and it was worth three dinars" — he is liable.
Let him say to him: "You already received it!"
phrases.notes: The borrower should argue that the lost משכון already counts as full payment, like שמואל said.

steps.triggerLanguage: תְּנַן: ״סֶלַע הִלְוִיתִיךָ עָלָיו וְשֶׁקֶל הָיָה שָׁוֶה״
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Goes back to שמואל's ruling and tests it against the משנה.
steps.kashyaTarget: שמואל's ruling that losing a cheap משכון cancels the whole loan.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The משנה keeps the borrower liable for the difference after a lost משכון worth less than the loan. Under שמואל, the debt should have been fully cancelled.

steps.title: The משנה is when the lender said so explicitly; שמואל is when he didn't
steps.stepSummary: The משנה is talking about a case where the lender said clearly that the משכון covers only its own value. שמואל is talking about a case where nothing was said.
steps.simpleTranslation: Our משנה is where he spelled it out; שמואל is where he did not spell it out.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by showing that the משנה and שמואל are talking about two different cases.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the lender said 'I am taking this only for its value,' then losing it only takes off its value, as in the משנה. If he said nothing, we assume a cheap item taken for a big loan was meant to stand for the whole loan, as שמואל ruled. So the משנה does not contradict שמואל.

keyTerms.meaning: Where he did not state it explicitly

steps.whatToRemember: שמואל's rule applies only when the lender took the משכון without saying anything. If he said it covers only its own value, losing it only takes off that value.

phrases.english: Our Mishnah is where he stated explicitly,
phrases.notes: He means the lender said the משכון only covers its own worth, not the whole loan.

phrases.english: Shmuel is where he did not state explicitly.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the משנה by separating the two cases.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splitting the cases (אוקימתא): the משנה and שמואל deal with different situations.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The משנה seemed to show that a lost cheap משכון never cancels the whole loan, which goes against שמואל.
steps.terutzMaskana: The משנה is where the lender said explicitly that the משכון covers only its value. שמואל is where nothing was said, so the משכון stands for the whole loan.

steps.title: Maybe this is an argument between רבי אליעזר and רבי עקיבא
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that שמואל's rule depends on an argument in a ברייתא. רבי אליעזר says the lender swears and collects. רבי עקיבא says a lost משכון means the lender's money is lost.
steps.simpleTranslation: Let us say this is an argument between תנאים. Someone lent money to his friend and took a משכון, and the משכון was lost. He swears and takes his money; this is the view of רבי אליעזר. רבי עקיבא says the borrower can tell him: 'You only lent me money because of the משכון! The משכון is lost, so your money is lost.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא and suggests that שמואל's rule is really an old argument. שמואל would match רבי עקיבא, and רבי אליעזר would disagree with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי אליעזר holds that the debt stays alive even after the משכון is lost. The lender only needs to swear that it really was lost, and then he collects. רבי עקיבא holds that the loan was tied to the משכון, so losing it cancels the debt, which looks just like שמואל's rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Let us say this is an argument between תנאים
Did you lend me anything (except on the משכון)?

steps.confusionAlert: לימא means 'let us say.' It is only a suggestion. Often the גמרא suggests linking an אמורא to a מחלוקת תנאים and then shows that the link is not needed.

phrases.english: Let us say it is like an argument between Tannaim:
phrases.notes: The גמרא is wondering if שמואל's rule from Step 6 is really this older argument.

phrases.english: One who lends to his fellow on collateral
and the collateral was lost
he swears and takes his money.
These are the words of Rabbi Eliezer.
Rabbi Akiva says,
he can say to him:
phrases.notes: 'He' is the borrower, speaking to the lender.

phrases.english: Did you lend me anything except on the collateral?
The collateral is lost, so your money is lost.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After the קשיא from the משנה was answered, the גמרא now asks whether שמואל's rule is the subject of an argument between תנאים.
steps.raayaObject: שמואל's rule that a lost משכון cancels the loan
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא in which רבי עקיבא says 'the משכון is lost, your money is lost,' against רבי אליעזר

steps.title: With a שטר, everyone agrees the money is lost
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא continues. If the lender had a שטר for 1,000 זוז and also held a משכון, everyone agrees that losing the משכון means losing the money.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if someone lent 1,000 זוז with a שטר, and the borrower also left a משכון with him, everyone agrees: the משכון is lost, so his money is lost.
steps.whatsHappening: The ברייתא adds a case where רבי אליעזר and רבי עקיבא both agree. If there was a שטר and also a משכון, losing the משכון cancels the debt.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The lender already had a שטר as proof of the loan, so the משכון was not needed as proof. That is why both sides agree it was taken as backing for repayment, and its loss wipes out the money. So the argument in Step 11 is only about a loan backed by a משכון alone.

keyTerms.meaning: And he left a משכון in his hand

phrases.english: But one who lends a thousand zuz with a document,
and he left collateral in his hand,
phrases.notes: The borrower left the משכון with the lender, in addition to the שטר.

phrases.english: everyone agrees:
the collateral is lost, so his money is lost.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: This continues the same ברייתא and marks a case where both תנאים agree.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: When there is a שטר and also a משכון, everyone agrees that losing the משכון means losing the loan money.

steps.title: What exact case are they arguing about?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what the case of the argument is. It begins with one option: the משכון was worth the full amount of the loan.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the case? If the משכון was worth the amount of the money that was lent...
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא starts to ask what exact case רבי אליעזר and רבי עקיבא argue about. This line sets up the next move, which will test this first option.
steps.deeperAnalysis: To know whether שמואל matches רבי עקיבא, the גמרא must pin down the case. The first option is a משכון worth the whole loan. The sentence stops in the middle, and its ending comes next.

keyTerms.meaning: What is the case? What are the details?
That it is worth the amount of the money

phrases.english: What is the case?
If it is worth the amount of the money,

steps.triggerLanguage: הֵיכִי דָמֵי? אִי דְּשָׁוֵי שִׁיעוּר זוּזֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: The גמרא now examines the ברייתא from Steps 11-12 to find the exact case of the argument.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How much the משכון was worth in the case where רבי אליעזר and רבי עקיבא argue
